4.2 — Enemy Animation: A Different State Machine

You wired the Player's animator, so you already know how animators work: a parameter goes in, a state comes out, and the code never touches the frames. Today you meet the enemy's animator — and it follows none of your conventions. Same API. Same method names. Completely different rules. Learning to read somebody else's state machine is the real lesson here, and it is the one that will save you in Unit 8.

The Problem: A Statue That Slides ~20 min

Your enemy patrols, but it slides around as a single frozen frame. The art exists and the animation controller exists — they were simply never connected to any code. Your job is to drive it. But before you write a line, you must find out what the animator wants, and the only place that is written down is the animator itself.

Step 1 — find the Animator. Select the MobileEnemy prefab and look at the child object. Which object carries the Animator component, and which carries the Sprite Renderer? Step 2 — open the Animator window and read the Parameters list. Step 3 — click the states and read every transition's conditions. Write down the exact names, types and numbers before you read any further.

Here is what you should have found, next to what you built yourself in Unit 1:

 The Player's animator (you built this)The enemy's animator (already in the project)
Parameters IsWalking (Bool), WalkDir (Int), Attack (Trigger) Direction (Int), Attack (Trigger)
What the Int means 0 = Up, 1 = Horizontal, 2 = Down 0 = Right, 1 = Up, 2 = Left, 3 = Down
Where the Animator lives A child object named Sprite A child object named Sprite
Idle states Yes. Your controller has idle states to fall back on when the player stops. None at all. The controller holds only Walk and Attack states. There is nowhere to go when the enemy stops.
Facing left and right One clip per direction, mirrored with flipX on the Sprite Renderer. Two separate clips — WalkLeft and WalkRight. This controller never touches flipX anywhere.
Attack A Trigger you set from your code. A Trigger you set from your code.
The names look familiar. The numbers do not. Both machines are driven with SetInteger. In yours, 0 means Up; in the enemy's, 0 means Right. A line copied from one script into the other compiles happily and produces an enemy that walks sideways when it should walk up. Two rules follow from this, and they are the point of today:
  • Before you drive any animator, read its parameters and its transitions. Never infer them from the scripts you have already written.
  • An Animator controller is a state machine with its own vocabulary. Two controllers that share an API share nothing else.
The three parameter types, and why Attack is a Trigger.
  • A Bool is a switch. You turn it on and you are responsible for turning it off. Forget the second half and the machine is stuck in that state forever.
  • An Int is a selector. It holds a value indefinitely, so whatever you set last is still true next frame — which is exactly why the enemy controller has no idle state: nothing ever tells it to stop.
  • A Trigger is a one-shot event. It fires once and resets itself, so you cannot forget to clear it. Attacks are events, not conditions — which is why both animators use a Trigger for them.

Socratic: Reading Someone Else's Machine

  1. Your player's WalkDir and the enemy's Direction are both Ints set by SetInteger. Before copying any animator line from one script to the other, what exactly must you check — and where do you check it?
  2. The enemy's controller has no idle states. If your code simply stops calling SetInteger when the enemy stops walking, what does the player see on screen — and is that a bug in your code or a gap in the asset?
  3. Your player mirrors one clip with flipX; the enemy uses two separate clips and never flips. What does the enemy's approach give you that yours cannot — and what does it cost?
  4. Attack is a Trigger, not a Bool. What happens if you model an attack with a Bool and forget to switch it off — and why does a Trigger make that mistake impossible?
  5. Which object on the MobileEnemy prefab carries the Animator, and which GetComponent family call reaches it from the root? What would the plain GetComponent<Animator>() return from the root?
  6. The four Idle clips — IdleUp, IdleDown, IdleLeft, IdleRight — exist as files in the Animations folder. Does their existence mean the enemy has idle states? What is the difference between an asset existing and an asset being wired?
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Read each snippet for what it does in isolation, then work out how it maps onto your enemy. None of these is from a video game.

Example 1 — A stage lighting desk firing the next cue:

// A cue button fires once and is forgotten; a dimmer is a switch you must reset
lighting.SetTrigger("NextCue");

Example 2 — A departure board selecting a platform:

// "0" means the northbound platform on THIS board and on no other board
board.SetInteger("Line", 0);

Example 3 — A parcel arm reaching its own mechanism, not the pallet:

// The controller is on the arm itself, one level below where this script sits
arm.GetComponentInChildren<Animator>().SetInteger("Side", 2);

Example 4 — A jukebox with no pause button (comment only):

// This machine only knows how to play a track. There is no silent state for
// it to return to, so stopping the music is something you must build.

Example 5 — A hotel lift panel (comment only):

// The panel is told which floor to travel to. It is never told "stay put" -
// staying put is simply the absence of a new instruction.

Predict Before Building

  1. Example 1 says a cue button is forgotten and a dimmer is not. Which of the enemy's two parameters behaves like the cue button, and which behaves like the dimmer?
  2. Example 2 says the code 0 means something only against the board that defines it. If you paste a line that sets Direction to 2 expecting "Down", what will the enemy actually do? Check the table.
  3. Example 3 reaches a component one level below. Why does the enemy root need the same trick, and what would happen instead of an error if a stray Animator existed on the root?
  4. Example 4 describes a machine with no silent state. Which single fact about the enemy's controller makes the same sentence true of your enemy?
  5. Example 5 says "stay put" is the absence of an instruction. If your code stops giving the enemy instructions, what does the animator keep doing — and why does the answer matter for a guard standing at the end of its beat?
Build Lab: Drive the Enemy's Animator ~25 min

Step 1 — choose your approach. There is a complete, working script at Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts/TopDown_EnemyAnimator.cs. It is not attached to anything. Read it before you decide anything: it is short, it is commented, and it was written by somebody else — which is exactly the skill this lesson is about. Then choose: attach that script, or write your own driver inside EnemyController.cs. Either is defensible. Write down which you picked and why.

Architectural specification for driving the enemy's animator:

Reaching the Animator:

  • Which object carries the Animator on the MobileEnemy prefab, and which GetComponent family call finds it from the root? What does the plain version return instead — a null, or the wrong component?
  • When should that lookup run: once at startup, or every frame? Which of the two did you do for the turret's target in 3.1, and why does the same reasoning apply?
  • If you chose the package script, where would you attach it so that its own lookup finds the Animator — and what does its Start() method assume about the object it sits on?

Computing a direction:

  • You have the animation parameter's contract: four integer values with a specific meaning. Which quantity in your enemy's movement tells you which of the four to set — the movement it was asked for, or the movement that actually happened?
  • The enemy can move on both axes and can have one axis larger than the other. How do you decide which of the four values wins on a diagonal step? Compare the sizes of the two components, not their values — why does that distinction matter when moving left?
  • Write out, in words, the mapping from "moving in this direction" to "this integer". Say where the 0 goes and where the 3 goes, and check it against the Parameters list rather than against your memory.
  • Which lifecycle method should set the parameter — the one that runs once per frame, or the one that runs once per physics step? What does the package script use, and does that make a visible difference?

The attack:

  • Attack is a Trigger. How often may you set it — and what happens on screen if you set it every frame?
  • Nothing in your enemy attacks yet. When 4.4 adds contact damage, where in that flow will the trigger be set, and what will the animator's Attack states need to line up with?
  • Should the animation decide when damage happens, or should damage decide when the animation plays? Argue a position — this is a real architectural fork and Unit 8 will test it.

Save, play, and watch a full beat. The enemy should face the way it walks, in all four directions, and stop animating only if you work out how to make it stop.

Bug Hunt: Wrong Machine, Wrong Rules

  1. Attach your animation driver to the enemy's root and press Play. What error appears, and which object actually holds the Animator?
  2. Never call SetInteger and simply watch the enemy move. What does the sprite do while Direction sits at its default value?
  3. Set Direction to 4 — a value no state uses. What happens? Why is a wrong-value bug with no error message harder to find than a crash?
  4. Call SetInteger("WalkDir", 1) on the enemy's animator — the parameter name your player uses. What appears in the Console, and what does that prove about parameter names?
  5. Try to face the enemy left by setting flipX on its Sprite Renderer, then walk it left. What do you see, and why does flipX do nothing useful on this rig?
  6. Call SetTrigger("Attack") every frame instead of once. What does the animation do — and which lesson's every-frame problem have you just recreated?
Tinker ~15 min

Tinker: Change the Rules

  1. The four Idle clips exist in the animations folder but the controller never uses them. What would you have to change — in the controller and in your code — before a standing enemy idles?
  2. Your player animates with one clip and flipX; the enemy uses two clips and never flips. If you had to support eight directions including diagonals, which approach scales better, and what would each one cost you in new animation clips?
  3. Add a Bool parameter to the enemy controller called IsChasing and drive it from your code. If no transition uses it, has anything changed on screen? What is a parameter with nothing attached to it worth?
  4. The package script fires an attack when the mouse button is held. What does that tell you about where it came from, and would you ship it in this game unchanged? Justify your answer in one sentence.
  5. Commit and push: "4.2: enemy animator driven from movement".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name the enemy's two animator parameters and their types, by reading the controller
  • Recite the four Direction values without looking — and say how they differ from your player's
  • Explain why the enemy's animator needs GetComponentInChildren
  • Explain what the enemy does visually when it stops, and why the controller has no answer for it
  • State that this controller uses separate left and right clips and never uses flipX
  • Explain the difference between an animation asset existing and being wired into the controller
  • Commit and push
